strava_runs <- read_csv("data/strava_runs.csv")
## Rows: 40471 Columns: 7
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr (2): gender, timestamp
## dbl (5): athlete, distance..m., elapsed.time..s., elevation.gain..m., averag...
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      distance..m. > 4998 & distance..m. < 5015  ~ "5k",
      distance..m. > 9998 & distance..m. < 10015 ~ "10k",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event))

Exercise 1

When you fill the missing part, remove the # symbol before running the code chunk and eval=FALSE

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "M") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  labs(
    title = "Average heart rate for male runners",
    x = "Average heart rate (bpm)",
    y = "Number of runs"
  )

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(gender == "M") %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)),
    mean_bpm = mean(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bpm = median(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_bpm = sd(average.heart.rate..bpm., na.rm = TRUE)
  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##       n mean_bpm median_bpm sd_bpm
##   <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1   252     148.       148.   17.2

The histogram is approximately unimodal and bell-shaped, with a main peak around 145–150 bpm. The mean (147.94 bpm) and median (147.90 bpm) are almost identical, supporting an approximately symmetric distribution. The standard deviation is 17.22 bpm. There is no clear evidence of separate clusters in this histogram. These statistics are based on 252 runs with non-missing heart rate measurements.

  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##       n mean_bpm median_bpm sd_bpm
##   <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1    76     156.       157.   13.2

The female histogram has several peaks and is less smooth than the male histogram. Female runs have a higher mean heart rate (155.68 bpm) than male runs (147.94 bpm). The standard deviation is smaller for females (13.22 versus 17.22 bpm), so their heart rates are less spread out. However, the two distributions overlap.

Exercise 2

Write your code to answer exercise 2a here

data_5k_10k %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%
  mutate(
    pace = (elapsed.time..s. / 60) / (distance..m. / 1000),
    event = factor(event, levels = c("5k", "10k"))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = event, y = pace)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ gender, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Running pace for 5k and 10k runs",
    subtitle = "F = Female, M = Male; lower pace means faster running",
    x = "Run distance",
    y = "Pace (minutes per km)"
  )

Male runs have a lower median pace than female runs at both distances, so they are generally faster in this dataset. For both genders, 10k runs have a slightly lower median pace than 5k runs. The 5k runs show more variation, with some much slower runs.

Exercise 3

# Write your code to answer exercise 3 here
runner_groups <- strava_runs %>%
  group_by(athlete) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance = mean(distance..m., na.rm = TRUE) / 1000
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    runner_type = case_when(
      mean_distance > 13 ~ "Long-distance runner",
      mean_distance < 7 ~ "Short-distance runner",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(runner_type))

runner_data <- strava_runs %>%
  inner_join(runner_groups, by = "athlete") %>%
  mutate(
    distance_km = distance..m. / 1000,
    speed = distance..m. / elapsed.time..s.
  )

ggplot(
  runner_data,
  aes(x = distance_km, y = speed, colour = runner_type)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Long-distance runner" = "orange",
      "Short-distance runner" = "forestgreen"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Speed vs Distance for Long- and Short-Distance Runners",
    subtitle = "Grouped by runners' average distance: >13 km vs <7 km",
    x = "Run distance (km)",
    y = "Run average speed (m/s)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Long-distance runners tend to run faster than short-distance runners at the same distance. Both lines slope downwards, but the decrease is greater for short-distance runners. This suggests that the two groups have different speed patterns, although their results overlap.
